task_1.title: Update removed deprecated Flask file-serving and context APIs
task_1.description: Flask 2.2.0 removes previously deprecated compatibility aliases in file-serving helpers and removes the request-context proxy for g. Applications upgrading from 2.1.3 must use the current argument names and stop depending on RequestContext.g behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that application code upgrading to Flask 2.2.0 no longer uses removed deprecated argument names in file-serving helpers and no longer depends on RequestContext.g as a proxy for application context state.

expectation.grounded: Calls to flask.send_file must use the supported keyword names download_name, max_age, and etag instead of the removed aliases attachment_filename, cache_timeout, and add_etags. Calls to flask.send_from_directory must use path instead of the removed filename alias. Code must not access or assign RequestContext.g and should rely on the standard application-context g object. When max_age is omitted or None in file-serving helpers, default cache lifetime resolution should continue through the app's configured send-file max-age behavior.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should preserve normal file download, caching, and ETag behavior when using the current public API names, while treating the old deprecated names as unsupported. Request-scoped shared state should be accessed through the standard g object only, not through a request-context proxy.

constraints.grounded: Supported behavior for send_file and send_from_directory using download_name, max_age, etag, and path must remain intact, including default max_age resolution when no explicit value is provided. The upgrade scope is limited to removing deprecated aliases and the RequestContext.g proxy behavior; no new public file-serving semantics should be introduced.
constraints.conceptual: Keep existing supported file-serving behavior unchanged for valid modern API usage. The change should only remove deprecated compatibility paths and require callers to use the current supported interfaces.

behavior: send_file supports download_name, max_age, and etag as the public argument names for attachment naming, cache lifetime, and ETag control.
Passing attachment_filename, cache_timeout, or add_etags to send_file is no longer supported and is no longer translated from deprecated names to the current API.
send_from_directory uses path as the supported file selector argument, and filename is no longer supported as an alias.
RequestContext.g no longer proxies to AppContext.g, so code must use the standard g object directly for shared context state.
If max_age is not provided to the file-serving helpers, they continue to use the application's default send-file max-age policy.
acceptance_criteria: When application code calls send_file with download_name, max_age, and etag, it should continue to serve files with the expected attachment, caching, and ETag behavior.
When application code attempts to call send_file with attachment_filename, cache_timeout, or add_etags, that usage should be considered unsupported after upgrading to Flask 2.2.0.
When application code calls send_from_directory, it should identify the target file using path rather than filename.
When code needs shared request/application state, it should access g directly instead of reading from or writing to RequestContext.g.
When no explicit max_age is supplied to send_file or send_from_directory, the response should still follow the application's default send-file cache lifetime policy.

task_2.title: Require Werkzeug 2.2.0 or newer
task_2.description: Version 2.2.0 raises the minimum supported Werkzeug dependency from the 2.0 line to 2.2.0 so installations and deployments use the supported Werkzeug baseline for this release.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to version 2.2.0 also upgrades the application's Werkzeug dependency to version 2.2.0 or newer so the library is installed and run only with the supported Werkzeug release line.

expectation.grounded: Version 2.2.0 must declare a minimum dependency of Werkzeug 2.2.0 or newer rather than Werkzeug 2.0 or newer. Dependency resolution and supported runtime environments for this release should therefore use Werkzeug >= 2.2.0, and versions below 2.2.0 are no longer supported with this release.
expectation.conceptual: The 2.2.0 upgrade should move consumers onto a newer supported Werkzeug baseline. After upgrading, the package should only be used in environments that provide a compatible Werkzeug version from 2.2 onward.

constraints.grounded: Keep the requirement limited to the dependency compatibility change evidenced by the release note and diff. Do not infer unrelated framework features, API changes, or behavior beyond the new minimum supported Werkzeug version.
constraints.conceptual: Treat this as a dependency support-floor update only. The requirement should not imply any separate end-user feature beyond requiring a newer compatible Werkzeug version.

behavior: The package's declared runtime dependency floor for Werkzeug changes from version 2.0 to version 2.2.0.
Installing or resolving dependencies for version 2.2.0 should treat Werkzeug versions earlier than 2.2.0 as incompatible.
Applications upgrading to version 2.2.0 must upgrade any pinned Werkzeug 2.0.x or 2.1.x dependency to a 2.2.0-or-newer release.
acceptance_criteria: When package dependency metadata for version 2.2.0 is inspected or resolved, it should advertise Werkzeug 2.2.0 or newer as the minimum supported version.
When version 2.2.0 is installed into an environment without a conflicting pin, dependency resolution should select a Werkzeug release that is at least 2.2.0.
When an environment remains pinned to a Werkzeug version below 2.2.0, that environment should be considered unsupported for version 2.2.0 until Werkzeug is upgraded.

task_4.title: Deprecate FLASK_ENV and app.env in favor of explicit debug control
task_4.description: Flask 2.2.0 deprecates environment-based debug selection through FLASK_ENV and app.env, and shifts users toward explicit debug control through --debug, FLASK_DEBUG, or app.run(debug=True). Legacy FLASK_ENV usage remains temporarily recognized for compatibility, but it now emits deprecation signals and should no longer be treated as the primary way to enable development behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that application debug behavior is controlled explicitly rather than by environment naming, and that legacy FLASK_ENV or app.env usage is treated as deprecated compatibility behavior with clear migration signals.

expectation.grounded: Flask 2.2 should deprecate app.env and flask.helpers.get_env(), emitting DeprecationWarning when they are accessed. Debug behavior should be driven by app.debug, the --debug CLI option, FLASK_DEBUG, or app.run(debug=True), not by app.env. If FLASK_ENV is still present, Flask may continue to derive a compatibility debug value from it, but it should emit a deprecation notice on stderr and treat FLASK_ENV as transitional behavior scheduled for removal in Flask 2.3. The flask run command should describe --debug as the way to enable the debugger and reloader by default.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should remove the idea that selecting an application environment is how users turn on development behavior. Users should enable debug mode directly, while any continued use of older environment-based switches should still work temporarily but clearly warn that they are deprecated and will be removed.

constraints.grounded: Existing public debug controls must continue to function: FLASK_DEBUG should still override debug mode, app.run(debug=...) should remain valid, and legacy FLASK_ENV handling should not silently disappear in 2.2. app.env must continue to map to the ENV config value during the deprecation period. Changing app.debug should only update Jinja template auto-reload when TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD has not been explicitly configured.
constraints.conceptual: The migration must preserve current ways to explicitly enable or disable debug mode, keep older environment-based usage temporarily compatible, and avoid overriding separate template reload settings that were intentionally configured by the user.

behavior: Accessing or assigning app.env produces a DeprecationWarning while still reading from or writing to the application's ENV configuration value.
Calling flask.helpers.get_env() produces a DeprecationWarning and continues to return the FLASK_ENV value when present, otherwise the production environment value.
When FLASK_DEBUG is unset, debug mode defaults to off instead of being implicitly enabled by a non-debug environment concept.

When FLASK_ENV is present without FLASK_DEBUG, Flask still derives compatibility debug behavior from FLASK_ENV and emits a deprecation notice to stderr indicating that FLASK_DEBUG should be used instead.
When FLASK_DEBUG is present, it remains the effective source of debug mode for flask run and app.run.
The flask run command documents --debug as the default trigger for the debugger and reloader rather than FLASK_ENV=development.
Updating app.debug only toggles Jinja auto-reload when template auto-reload has not already been explicitly configured.
acceptance_criteria: When a user enables debug mode with --debug, FLASK_DEBUG, or app.run(debug=True), the development server should run with debugger and reload behavior without requiring app.env or FLASK_ENV.
When application code reads or writes app.env, it should continue to work for the current release but emit a DeprecationWarning.
When application code calls flask.helpers.get_env(), it should continue to return an environment value for the current release but emit a DeprecationWarning.
When FLASK_ENV is set and FLASK_DEBUG is not set, starting the app should emit a deprecation notice and only use FLASK_ENV as temporary compatibility input for debug behavior.
When neither --debug nor FLASK_DEBUG is provided, debug mode should not become enabled merely because of a default environment distinction.
When TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD is explicitly configured, changing app.debug should not override that template reload setting.

task_3.title: Migrate Flask context access to the 2.2 ContextVar model
task_3.description: Flask 2.2.0 replaces LocalStack-backed app and request context management with direct ContextVar tracking for lower overhead while keeping current-context access working through proxies. Applications and extensions should stop relying on _app_ctx_stack.top and _request_ctx_stack.top for extension state, move that state to g, and use the current app or request context proxies that remain valid under the new model.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications and extensions upgrading to Flask 2.2 no longer depend on `_app_ctx_stack.top` or `_request_ctx_stack.top` as the primary way to read or store per-context state, and instead use `g`, `current_app`, `request`, `session`, `app_ctx`, or `request_ctx` so request and application context behavior remains correct under the new context management model.

expectation.grounded: Flask 2.2 must manage `AppContext` and `RequestContext` through direct context variables while preserving the observable behavior of `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session` within active contexts. `flask.globals.app_ctx` and `flask.globals.request_ctx` should expose the current context objects through proxies. Access to `flask._app_ctx_stack`, `flask._request_ctx_stack`, or their `.top` values should remain available only as deprecated compatibility shims that emit `DeprecationWarning`, and extension state should be stored on `g` instead of stack-top objects.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading, context-aware code should continue to work through Flask’s normal context proxies, but code that treats the old context stacks as stable public storage should be considered deprecated and migrated to the supported context APIs.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress the ability to access `current_app`, `g`, `request`, or `session` during an active app or request context. A request context must still create an implicit app context when needed and restore the previous active context when popped or copied. Deprecated stack access may warn, but it must not disappear outright in 2.2, and request-context helpers such as `after_this_request`, `copy_current_request_context`, and `stream_with_context` must continue to require an active request context.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should preserve existing request and application context behavior for supported APIs, while surfacing deprecations instead of silently breaking current-context access. Any migration away from the old stack objects must keep nested, copied, and streamed request flows behaving consistently.

behavior: Flask now binds the active application and request contexts through context variables instead of Werkzeug `LocalStack`, which changes the internal storage model but keeps `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session` resolving against the current context.
New `app_ctx` and `request_ctx` proxies provide access to the active `AppContext` and `RequestContext` objects without using the deprecated stack-top API.
Importing or accessing `_app_ctx_stack` and `_request_ctx_stack`, including reading `.top`, remains possible in 2.2 only through deprecated compatibility objects and emits `DeprecationWarning`.
Per-extension or per-context data that was previously stored on `_app_ctx_stack.top` or `_request_ctx_stack.top` is expected to move to `g` with an extension-specific attribute name.

`after_this_request`, `copy_current_request_context`, and `stream_with_context` raise `RuntimeError` when no request context is active, and streamed iteration keeps the request context available while the stream is being consumed.

Request teardown still occurs when the final request-context pop happens, and debugger or preserved-context integrations keep access to the current contexts through the new preservation path rather than the old preserved stack state.
acceptance_criteria: When code runs inside an active Flask request or app context, it should be able to use `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session` normally without depending on `_app_ctx_stack.top` or `_request_ctx_stack.top`.

When extension code accesses `_app_ctx_stack` or `_request_ctx_stack` in Flask 2.2, it should still receive a compatibility object for the current release, but that access should emit `DeprecationWarning`.

When a request context is pushed for an app that does not already have an active app context, Flask should still create the corresponding app context and tear it down when the request context is fully popped.

When `after_this_request`, `copy_current_request_context`, or `stream_with_context` are used without an active request context, they should fail with `RuntimeError` rather than behaving as if a context exists.
When a streamed response or template is generated from within an active request, request-bound proxies should remain usable for the lifetime of that stream iteration.

task_7.title: Adopt Flask 2.2 JSON provider customization
task_7.description: Flask 2.2.0 introduces a pluggable JSON provider API centered on app.json and deprecates JSON customization through legacy config keys and app or blueprint encoder and decoder hooks. Applications upgrading from 2.1.3 should move JSON serialization, parsing, response formatting, and mimetype customization to the provider model while preserving existing behavior during the deprecation window.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the application remains compatible with Flask 2.2.0 by migrating JSON customization to the new provider-based API, preserving expected JSON serialization and parsing behavior, and handling deprecated JSON configuration and encoder or decoder hooks without breaking existing runtime behavior.

expectation.grounded: Flask 2.2.0 should expose application JSON behavior through app.json, an instance of Flask.json_provider_class. Custom JSON implementations should be supported by subclassing flask.json.provider.JSONProvider and providing dumps and loads behavior, with response generation available through app.json.response. The active provider should govern Flask JSON operations used by flask.json helpers, jsonify, the template tojson filter, request JSON loading, response JSON access, and test client JSON handling. On the default provider, JSON_AS_ASCII, JSON_SORT_KEYS, JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR, and JSONIFY_MIMETYPE are deprecated in favor of app.json.ensure_ascii, app.json.sort_keys, app.json.compact, and app.json.mimetype. Customization through app or blueprint json_encoder and json_decoder should remain functional in 2.2.0 but emit deprecation warnings and be treated as transitional behavior.
expectation.conceptual: JSON behavior should be customizable through a single application-level provider object so that serialization, deserialization, JSON responses, and related framework features stay consistent. Existing legacy JSON settings should continue to work during upgrade, but the supported long-term contract is to configure JSON behavior through the provider rather than through legacy config flags or encoder and decoder hooks.

constraints.grounded: The upgrade must preserve the default provider's externally visible JSON behavior unless intentionally overridden through provider attributes: ASCII escaping and key sorting remain enabled by default, JSON responses use the provider mimetype, and response formatting stays compact by default except when compact is false or debug mode causes readable formatting. app.json.response must continue to serialize no arguments as null, one positional argument as that value, multiple positional arguments as a JSON array, and keyword arguments as a JSON object, while rejecting mixed positional and keyword arguments with TypeError. Deprecated config keys and json_encoder or json_decoder hooks must not become immediate hard failures in 2.2.0. Non-default providers must not be assumed to support DefaultJSONProvider-specific options or deprecated config compatibility.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should not silently change how normal JSON payloads are produced or parsed unless an application explicitly opts into different provider behavior. Compatibility with older JSON customization paths should remain transitional rather than breaking immediately, and custom provider implementations should only be expected to honor the core provider contract, not legacy default-provider-specific knobs.

behavior: Flask 2.2.0 centralizes JSON operations on app.json and allows applications to replace JSON behavior either by assigning app.json directly or by setting Flask.json_provider_class.

Custom JSON providers are defined through the JSONProvider interface, with dumps and loads as the required serialization and deserialization entry points and response generation available through the provider.

jsonify and other Flask JSON entry points should use the active provider so that serialization, parsing, template JSON rendering, request JSON loading, response JSON access, and test client JSON behavior stay aligned.
On the default provider, app.json.ensure_ascii and app.json.sort_keys replace JSON_AS_ASCII and JSON_SORT_KEYS as the supported way to control string escaping and object key ordering.
On the default provider, app.json.compact and app.json.mimetype replace JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR and JSONIFY_MIMETYPE as the supported way to control JSON response formatting and Content-Type.

Using deprecated JSON config keys or app or blueprint json_encoder or json_decoder remains supported in 2.2.0 for compatibility, but it should emit DeprecationWarning and direct users toward provider-based customization.
JSON responses remain compact by default, switch to readable formatting when compact is false, and also use readable formatting when compact is unset and the application is in debug mode.

app.json.response preserves argument-shape semantics by serializing no arguments as null, a single positional argument as that value, multiple positional arguments as a list, keyword arguments as an object, and by rejecting calls that mix positional and keyword arguments.
acceptance_criteria: When an application assigns a custom app.json provider or sets Flask.json_provider_class, Flask JSON serialization, deserialization, and JSON response generation should use that provider consistently.

When JSON is produced through jsonify, rendered through the template tojson filter, parsed from request JSON, or accessed through response or test client JSON helpers, the behavior should follow the active application JSON provider.

When app.json.response is called with no arguments, it should serialize null; with one positional argument, it should serialize that value; with multiple positional arguments, it should serialize a JSON array; with keyword arguments, it should serialize a JSON object; and when both positional and keyword arguments are passed, it should raise TypeError.
When the default provider's ensure_ascii, sort_keys, compact, or mimetype settings are changed, serialized output and JSON response behavior should reflect those provider settings.

When legacy JSON config keys or app or blueprint json_encoder or json_decoder hooks are used during the upgrade, the application should continue to function but should emit deprecation warnings indicating that provider-based JSON customization is now the supported path.
When compact is false, or when compact is unset and the application runs in debug mode, JSON responses should use readable pretty formatting; otherwise JSON responses should remain compact.

task_5.title: Migrate deprecated Flask app config proxy attributes
task_5.description: Flask 2.2.0 deprecates several app-level shortcut attributes in favor of reading and writing the corresponding app.config keys directly. The upgrade should preserve existing runtime behavior for session cookies, send_file defaults, X-Sendfile handling, template auto reload, and exception propagation while avoiding reliance on APIs scheduled for removal in Flask 2.3.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to Flask 2.2.0 stop depending on deprecated Flask app shortcut attributes and instead rely on the corresponding configuration entries, without changing observable session, file-serving, template reload, or exception propagation behavior.

expectation.grounded: In Flask 2.2, `Flask.session_cookie_name`, `Flask.send_file_max_age_default`, `Flask.use_x_sendfile`, `Flask.propagate_exceptions`, and `Flask.templates_auto_reload` remain available only as deprecated compatibility surfaces. Reading or setting these attributes should continue to reflect `app.config["SESSION_COOKIE_NAME"]`, `app.config["SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT"]`, `app.config["USE_X_SENDFILE"]`, `app.config["PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS"]`, and `app.config["TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD"]` respectively, while emitting `DeprecationWarning` and signaling removal in Flask 2.3. Runtime consumers such as session cookie naming, `send_file` max-age resolution, X-Sendfile support, Jinja auto-reload, and exception propagation should derive their behavior from configuration values directly.
expectation.conceptual: Treat these Flask settings as configuration values rather than stable app attributes. Deprecated attribute access may still function during the 2.2 transition, but the application should behave the same while using the config-based interface that will continue to work in later releases.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the effective behavior of the related settings during migration: `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` remains the source of truth for the session cookie name; `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT` continues to support `None`, integer seconds, and `timedelta`-style values for default cache lifetime; `USE_X_SENDFILE` continues to control X-Sendfile usage for `send_file`; `TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD` still falls back to `app.debug` when unset; and `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` still falls back to `app.testing or app.debug` when unset.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must not change user-visible request handling, caching behavior, cookie naming, or template reload behavior. Only the supported configuration surface is changing; the runtime contract should remain stable.

behavior: Accessing or assigning deprecated app shortcut attributes for session cookie name, send-file max age, X-Sendfile, and template auto reload continues to work in 2.2 but emits `DeprecationWarning`.
Reading the deprecated `propagate_exceptions` attribute continues to work in 2.2 but emits `DeprecationWarning` and reflects the configured or fallback propagation behavior.
Session cookie naming is resolved from `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` in `app.config` rather than depending on `app.session_cookie_name` internally.

Default `send_file` and static-file max-age behavior is resolved from `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT` in `app.config`; `None` preserves conditional-request behavior, `timedelta` values are converted to seconds, and integer values are used directly.
X-Sendfile behavior for `send_file` is controlled from `USE_X_SENDFILE` in `app.config`.

Jinja template auto-reload is driven by `TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD` when explicitly configured, and otherwise falls back to `app.debug`; changing `app.debug` only updates Jinja auto-reload automatically when `TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD` is unset.
Exception propagation is determined by `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` when configured, and otherwise falls back to `app.testing` or `app.debug`.
acceptance_criteria: When an upgraded application customizes `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME`, the session system should use that configured cookie name without requiring `app.session_cookie_name`.

When code reads or writes `session_cookie_name`, `send_file_max_age_default`, `use_x_sendfile`, or `templates_auto_reload` on the Flask app in 2.2, it should still function but emit `DeprecationWarning`.
When code reads `propagate_exceptions` on the Flask app in 2.2, it should return the effective propagation setting and emit `DeprecationWarning`.
When `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT` is `None`, file responses should keep using conditional requests instead of a timed cache by default.
When `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT` is configured as integer seconds or as a duration value, default file response cache lifetime should reflect that configured duration.
When `USE_X_SENDFILE` is enabled, `send_file` should honor that setting through the config value.
When `TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD` is unset, template auto reload should track debug mode; when it is explicitly set, that explicit value should take precedence.
When `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` is unset, exception propagation should continue to follow testing/debug defaults; when it is explicitly set, that configured value should control propagation.

task_6.title: Adopt Flask 2.2 app-scoped helper and JSON provider customization
task_6.description: Flask 2.2 moves key helper behavior onto the application object so apps can override URL generation, redirects, abort handling, and JSON processing. The upgrade also introduces an app-scoped JSON provider model that centralizes serialization, deserialization, and JSON response behavior, while marking older encoder, decoder, and JSON config customization paths as deprecated.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that a Flask 2.2 application can customize URL building, redirects, abort handling, and JSON behavior at the app level, and that the public Flask helpers consistently delegate to those app-scoped customization points while preserving documented fallback and deprecation behavior.

expectation.grounded: Provide app-level customization through `Flask.url_for`, `Flask.redirect`, `Flask.aborter`, `Flask.aborter_class`, `Flask.make_aborter`, and `app.json` backed by `Flask.json_provider_class`. Within an active app context, `flask.url_for` must call `current_app.url_for`, `flask.redirect` must call `current_app.redirect`, `flask.abort` must call `current_app.aborter`, and `flask.json.dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, `load`, and `jsonify` must route through `app.json`. The default JSON provider must continue to support standard Flask JSON behavior, including JSON responses from `jsonify` and automatic JSON responses for view-returned `dict` and `list` values, while treating legacy `json_encoder`, `json_decoder`, `JSONEncoder`, `JSONDecoder`, and the deprecated JSON config keys as compatibility paths with deprecation warnings rather than the primary extension mechanism.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to override core helper behavior from the Flask app instance instead of relying on fixed global helper implementations. JSON handling should be centralized behind a per-application provider so serialization, deserialization, and JSON response generation all follow the active app's configured behavior consistently.

constraints.grounded: Outside an active app context, `flask.redirect` and `flask.abort` must continue to fall back to Werkzeug behavior, and `flask.json.dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, and `load` must continue to work through Python's standard `json` module. `jsonify` and `app.json.response` must reject mixed positional and keyword payload arguments with `TypeError`. Supplying `_scheme` to `url_for` must imply an external URL when `_external` is omitted, but combining `_scheme` with `_external=False` must raise `ValueError`. Deprecated JSON config keys are only compatibility shims for the default provider and are not required behavior for alternative providers.
constraints.conceptual: The new extension points must not remove default helper behavior when no application override is active. Error handling and fallback behavior should remain predictable, and deprecated JSON customization options should remain transitional compatibility features rather than required contracts for all JSON implementations.

behavior: `Flask` now exposes app-level hooks for URL generation, redirect creation, and abort handling, allowing helper calls to follow application-defined behavior.

`flask.url_for` delegates to the active app's `url_for` method, and providing `_scheme` without `_external` now produces an external URL automatically; explicitly setting `_external=False` with `_scheme` raises `ValueError`.
`flask.redirect` uses `app.redirect` when an application is active and otherwise falls back to Werkzeug redirect handling.
`flask.abort` uses `app.aborter` when an application is active and otherwise falls back to Werkzeug abort handling.
`app.json` is now the central JSON provider for an application, and `flask.json.dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, `load`, and `jsonify` use that provider whenever an app context is active.

JSON responses generated through `jsonify` or by returning a `dict` or `list` from a view are produced through the active app JSON provider, so response formatting and mimetype become provider-controlled behavior.
Template JSON serialization and request/response JSON parsing are aligned to the application's JSON provider instead of being hard-wired to the previous global JSON implementation.
Legacy JSON customization through encoder and decoder classes, helper `app` parameters, and the older JSON config keys remains available only as deprecated compatibility behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When an application overrides `app.url_for`, calling `flask.url_for` in that application context should use the overridden URL-building behavior.
When `url_for` is called with `_scheme` and `_external` is omitted, it should generate an external URL; when `_scheme` is combined with `_external=False`, it should raise `ValueError`.

When an application overrides `app.redirect` or configures a custom `app.aborter`, `flask.redirect` and `flask.abort` should follow the app-defined behavior inside the app context, and outside an app context they should continue to use default Werkzeug behavior.
When an application installs a custom `app.json` provider, Flask JSON helper functions and `jsonify` should use that provider while the app context is active.
When a view returns a `dict` or `list`, Flask should create the JSON response through the active app JSON provider rather than through a fixed global serializer.
When `jsonify` or `app.json.response` is called with both positional and keyword payload data, it should fail with `TypeError` instead of producing an ambiguous response.

When legacy JSON encoder or decoder customization paths, deprecated helper `app` parameters, or deprecated JSON config keys are used, they should remain backward-compatible for now but behave as deprecated compatibility paths rather than the preferred customization interface.

task_8.title: Adopt Flask's app-level JSON provider interface
task_8.description: Flask 2.2.0 adds an application-scoped JSON provider interface through `app.json` and `Flask.json_provider_class`, so JSON serialization, deserialization, and JSON response generation can be customized consistently across the app. Legacy JSON encoder and decoder hooks and related JSON config keys remain temporarily compatible under the default provider but are deprecated, so upgrades should move JSON customization to the provider interface while preserving existing observable JSON behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Flask 2.2.0 uses the new app-level JSON provider model for JSON customization, while preserving existing JSON serialization, deserialization, and `jsonify` behavior and treating older encoder, decoder, and JSON config hooks as deprecated compatibility paths.

expectation.grounded: Expose JSON customization through `Flask.json_provider_class` and the `app.json` provider instance. When an app context is active, `flask.json.dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, and `load` must delegate to the active provider, and `jsonify`, the Jinja `|tojson` filter, and request JSON parsing must use the same provider-backed behavior. `DefaultJSONProvider` must continue Flask's built-in handling for extra serializable types such as `datetime.date` and `datetime.datetime`, `decimal.Decimal`, `uuid.UUID`, dataclasses, and objects implementing `__html__`. Using `Flask.json_encoder`, `Flask.json_decoder`, `Blueprint.json_encoder`, `Blueprint.json_decoder`, `flask.json.JSONEncoder`, `flask.json.JSONDecoder`, the `app` parameter on `flask.json.dumps` / `dump` / `loads` / `load`, and the JSON config keys `JSON_AS_ASCII`, `JSON_SORT_KEYS`, `JSONIFY_MIMETYPE`, and `JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR` should still work for compatibility where supported but emit deprecation warnings in favor of provider-based configuration.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to replace or extend Flask's JSON behavior from one app-level integration point, and all standard JSON entry points should honor that customization consistently. Existing applications should keep working during the upgrade, but older JSON customization mechanisms should clearly signal that they are transitional and should be migrated away from.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress default JSON behavior for applications that do not install a custom provider. Outside an app context, `flask.json` helper functions must continue to fall back to standard JSON operations, with Flask's default extra-type serialization still applied for dumping. `app.json.response` must preserve the existing payload contract by accepting either positional arguments or keyword arguments, serializing no arguments as `null`, and rejecting mixed positional and keyword input with a `TypeError`. Non-default providers are not required to honor deprecated JSON config keys.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should not silently change JSON payload semantics for applications staying on Flask's default JSON implementation. JSON customization should be consistent at the application level, backward compatibility should remain available during the transition, and deprecated settings should not be treated as the long-term contract.

behavior: Flask applications gain an `app.json` provider instance, created from `Flask.json_provider_class`, as the primary public customization point for JSON behavior.
Within an active app context, `flask.json.dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, and `load` route through the active provider instead of reading encoder and decoder settings directly.

The default provider preserves Flask's extra serialization support for HTTP-date rendering of date and datetime values, string conversion of `decimal.Decimal` and `uuid.UUID`, dataclass conversion to dictionaries, and string conversion of objects with `__html__`.

Legacy app-level and blueprint-level JSON encoder and decoder classes remain temporarily honored by `DefaultJSONProvider`, but using them raises `DeprecationWarning` and they are no longer the preferred extension mechanism.

Legacy JSON config keys for ASCII escaping, key sorting, JSON response mimetype, and pretty-printing remain temporarily honored by `DefaultJSONProvider`, but using them raises `DeprecationWarning` and provider attributes become the supported control surface.

Provider-driven JSON responses treat one positional argument as the response value, multiple positional arguments as a list, keyword arguments as an object, no arguments as `null`, and mixed positional plus keyword arguments as an error.
acceptance_criteria: When an application installs a custom `app.json` provider or customizes `Flask.json_provider_class`, Flask JSON helpers used under that app context should serialize and deserialize through that provider rather than through legacy encoder or decoder hooks.

When `jsonify` or other standard Flask JSON entry points are used in an application with a custom provider, the observable JSON output and response formatting controls should follow the provider's behavior.
When an application continues using the default JSON provider, Flask should still serialize supported extra Python types the same way as before the upgrade.

When legacy JSON customization APIs or deprecated JSON config keys are used, the application should continue to function through the compatibility path but emit `DeprecationWarning` instead of failing silently.
When JSON helper functions are called without an active Flask app context, they should still perform JSON serialization and parsing with fallback behavior rather than requiring an app instance.
When a JSON response is built with both positional and keyword payload arguments, it should raise `TypeError`; when built with no payload, it should serialize `null`.

task_9.title: Adopt Flask 2.2 JSON provider behavior
task_9.description: Flask 2.2.0 introduces an application-level JSON provider interface, routes JSON helper behavior through that provider, and deprecates legacy HTML-safe JSON helpers and older encoder or decoder customization patterns. Upgrading code should rely on the new provider-based JSON contract so custom serialization, response generation, and JSON parsing continue to behave correctly.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading from Flask 2.1.3 to 2.2.0 use the new app-level JSON provider contract for JSON serialization, deserialization, and JSON responses, while avoiding newly deprecated JSON helper and encoder or decoder customization APIs.

expectation.grounded: Flask 2.2.0 should expose JSON behavior through `app.json`, an instance of `Flask.json_provider_class`, based on `flask.json.provider.JSONProvider`. Public JSON entry points such as `flask.json.dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, and `load` should use the active app provider when an application context is available, `jsonify` should delegate response creation to `current_app.json.response`, and customization should be performed through the provider interface rather than `json_encoder`, `json_decoder`, `JSONEncoder`, or `JSONDecoder`. Calls to `flask.json.htmlsafe_dumps` and `flask.json.htmlsafe_dump` should be treated as deprecated in favor of Jinja's built-in HTML-safe JSON support.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, JSON behavior should be configurable at the application level through a dedicated provider object. JSON serialization, parsing, and JSON response generation should consistently follow that provider so apps can replace or optimize JSON handling without relying on legacy encoder or decoder hooks. Deprecated HTML-safe JSON helper APIs should no longer be the supported integration point.

constraints.grounded: The upgrade must preserve the public behavior of JSON helpers while allowing provider overrides to control response serialization. `jsonify` must continue returning a Flask `Response` with JSON content, but its serialization and formatting should come from `app.json.response`. Deprecated config-based formatting and mimetype options on the default provider may still exist for compatibility, but alternative providers are not required to support those default-provider-only options.
constraints.conceptual: The change should not remove normal JSON response behavior for applications that do not customize JSON handling, and it should not require consumers to depend on internal implementation details. Custom JSON behavior should be centralized at the app level and remain compatible with standard request and response flows.

behavior: Calling `flask.json.htmlsafe_dumps` emits a deprecation warning and continues producing HTML-safe JSON output.
Calling `flask.json.htmlsafe_dump` emits a deprecation warning and writes HTML-safe JSON using the deprecated helper path.
Calling `jsonify` now delegates JSON response construction to `current_app.json.response`, making provider overrides observable at runtime.
An application's configured JSON provider can change how Flask serializes and parses JSON across helper functions and JSON responses when an app context is active.
acceptance_criteria: When an application assigns a custom `Flask.json_provider_class` or `app.json`, JSON serialization and JSON response generation should follow that provider's behavior during request or application-context execution.
When `jsonify` is used under Flask 2.2.0, it should return a JSON `Response` whose serialization is controlled by the active app's JSON provider rather than hard-coded helper logic.
When code calls `flask.json.htmlsafe_dumps` or `flask.json.htmlsafe_dump`, it should still work but should surface deprecation signaling to indicate those APIs are being removed.
When upgrading existing JSON customization, supported application-level customization should rely on the JSON provider interface instead of legacy encoder or decoder attributes and classes.

task_10.title: Align error handler registration with Flask 2.2 validation behavior
task_10.description: Flask 2.2.0 refines `register_error_handler` input validation so invalid registrations are checked consistently through the shared exception-resolution path. Applications upgrading from 2.1.3 need to align with the new behavior for exception instances, non-`Exception` classes, and unknown HTTP status codes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that application error handler registration follows Flask 2.2.0 validation rules so invalid handler targets are rejected consistently and valid exception classes or recognized HTTP error codes continue to register normally.

expectation.grounded: Calls to `register_error_handler` must accept either a recognized HTTP status code or an exception class derived from `Exception`. Passing an exception instance must fail with `TypeError`. Passing a class that is not a subclass of `Exception` must fail with `ValueError`. Passing an unrecognized integer HTTP code must fail with `ValueError` rather than being treated as a valid registration input.
expectation.conceptual: The error-handler registration API should only accept valid exception classes or known HTTP error codes. Invalid inputs should be rejected deterministically with user-visible errors that reflect whether the caller passed an instance, an unsupported class, or an unknown status code.

constraints.grounded: Valid registrations for subclasses of `Exception` must still succeed, and subclasses of `HTTPException` must continue to resolve by their HTTP code. The change must preserve normal handler lookup and invocation for supported registrations while only altering validation and failure behavior for invalid inputs.
constraints.conceptual: This update should tighten input validation without regressing normal error handling. Existing valid handlers should behave the same after registration, and only unsupported registration inputs should change outcome.

behavior: `register_error_handler` now relies on the shared exception/code resolution path for validation instead of special-casing only `HTTPException` instances.
Passing any exception instance, including an `HTTPException` instance, is rejected because handlers can only be registered for classes or HTTP status codes.
Passing a class that does not inherit from `Exception` is rejected as invalid registration input.
Passing an unknown integer HTTP status code is rejected with `ValueError` instead of `KeyError`.
Passing a valid `HTTPException` subclass continues to associate the handler with that exception class and its HTTP status code.
acceptance_criteria: When `register_error_handler` receives a valid custom exception class derived from `Exception`, it should register the handler successfully.
When `register_error_handler` receives an exception instance instead of a class, it should raise `TypeError` and not register a handler.
When `register_error_handler` receives a class that is not a subclass of `Exception`, it should raise `ValueError` and not register a handler.
When `register_error_handler` receives an integer that is not a recognized HTTP error code, it should raise `ValueError` and not register a handler.
When a handler is registered for a valid `HTTPException` subclass or recognized HTTP error code, request-time error handling should continue to dispatch that handler normally.

task_13.title: Add reusable class-based view instances
task_13.description: Flask 2.2.0 adds an opt-in way for class-based views to reuse a single view instance across requests instead of constructing a new instance every time. This reduces repeated initialization work for views with expensive setup while keeping the existing per-request instantiation behavior as the default.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that class-based views can opt out of per-request instantiation so expensive setup can run once per generated view, while preserving the existing default behavior and making the reuse semantics safe and explicit.

expectation.grounded: Add the `View.init_every_request` class attribute with a default value of `True`. `View.as_view()` must continue to create a new instance for each request unless a subclass sets `init_every_request = False`, in which case the generated view reuses one instance for all requests created from that `as_view()` call. URL rule variables must still be delivered to `dispatch_request`, and `MethodView` must continue dispatching to the handler matching `request.method`, with `HEAD` falling back to `get` when no `head` handler exists.
expectation.conceptual: Class-based views should support an opt-in performance mode that reuses one view object across requests. By default, views should keep their current request-isolated lifecycle. Reused views must still handle routed parameters and HTTP method dispatch normally.

constraints.grounded: The default lifecycle must remain unchanged for subclasses that do not set `init_every_request` or leave it `True`. When reuse is enabled, request-specific data must not be treated as safe to store on `self`; request-scoped state should remain isolated from the shared instance. Method dispatch behavior and inferred allowed methods for `MethodView` subclasses must remain consistent with the defined or inherited HTTP verb handlers.
constraints.conceptual: The optimization must be opt-in and non-breaking by default. Enabling reuse must not change route matching or supported HTTP methods, and it must not encourage cross-request leakage of request-local state.

behavior: A `View` subclass may declare `init_every_request = False` to make the view created by `as_view()` reuse a single instance across requests.
When `init_every_request` is left at its default or set to `True`, each request continues to instantiate a fresh view object before calling `dispatch_request`.
When instance reuse is enabled, constructor side effects and expensive initialization tied to view creation occur once for that generated view instead of once per request.

Reused view instances continue to receive routed URL variables in `dispatch_request`, and `MethodView` verb handlers continue to be resolved from the incoming HTTP method, with `HEAD` using `get` if no dedicated `head` handler is defined.
acceptance_criteria: When a class-based view does not set `init_every_request`, repeated requests to the registered endpoint should continue to use separate view instances.
When a class-based view sets `init_every_request = False`, repeated requests to the same registered endpoint should reuse one view instance rather than re-running view construction on every request.
When instance reuse is enabled, routed URL variables should still reach `dispatch_request` and produce the same response behavior as before.
When a `MethodView` subclass defines HTTP verb handlers, requests should still dispatch to the matching handler, and a `HEAD` request should use the `get` handler if no `head` handler is implemented.

task_12.title: Migrate away from deprecated first-request setup hooks
task_12.description: Flask 2.2 deprecates application and blueprint setup that waits for the first request. Setup code should run during application creation or blueprint registration instead. The legacy first-request decorators still work in 2.2, but they now warn when registered and remain only as transitional compatibility before removal.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that application and blueprint initialization no longer depends on first-request hooks, and that setup logic runs during application creation or blueprint registration instead of waiting for the first incoming request.

expectation.grounded: Treat `Flask.before_first_request` and `Blueprint.before_app_first_request` as deprecated in Flask 2.2. Registering either hook should emit a `DeprecationWarning`, while still registering the callback. In 2.2, registered callbacks must continue to execute exactly once before the first request for a given application instance. Blueprint code that previously relied on `before_app_first_request` should move that setup to registration time, such as `Blueprint.record_once`.
expectation.conceptual: Applications upgrading to 2.2 should stop using first-request decorators for setup. Initialization should happen when the app is created, and blueprint-specific setup should happen when the blueprint is registered. Deprecated hooks may still work temporarily, but they should no longer be the supported way to initialize application state.

constraints.grounded: Keep transitional compatibility in 2.2 for already-registered first-request callbacks: they should still run through normal request dispatch and preserve once-per-application-instance behavior. Registration of deprecated hooks must warn, and concurrent first requests must not cause the same callback to execute more than once for one application instance.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should preserve legacy behavior only long enough to support migration, without allowing setup to remain request-triggered as the recommended pattern. Existing apps should continue to behave consistently while being guided toward setup-time initialization.

behavior: Applying the `Flask.before_first_request` decorator emits a `DeprecationWarning` at registration time and still registers the callback.
Applying the `Blueprint.before_app_first_request` decorator emits a `DeprecationWarning` at registration time and still arranges for the callback to run before the application's first request.
Deprecated first-request callbacks continue to execute only once per application instance during request handling.
Concurrent first requests against the same application instance must not cause deprecated first-request callbacks to run multiple times.
Setup logic should be moved from first-request callbacks to application creation or blueprint registration for forward compatibility.
acceptance_criteria: When an application registers a function with `Flask.before_first_request`, it should receive a deprecation warning and the function should still run once before that application instance handles its first request.

When a blueprint registers a function with `Blueprint.before_app_first_request`, it should receive a deprecation warning and the function should still run once before the application's first request after the blueprint is registered.
When multiple first requests race against the same application instance, deprecated first-request callbacks should execute at most once for that instance.
When setup code is moved to application creation or blueprint registration, application startup behavior should no longer depend on an initial request arriving.

task_11.title: Enforce setup before first request or blueprint registration
task_11.description: Flask 2.2.0 tightens lifecycle enforcement for setup APIs. Application setup calls now fail after the first handled request regardless of debug mode, blueprint setup calls now warn after a blueprint has been registered, and blueprint first-request setup usage is deprecated so configuration must happen earlier and more consistently.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that all application and blueprint routes, handlers, template helpers, and other setup-time registrations are completed before the app serves its first request or a blueprint is registered, and stop relying on deprecated blueprint first-request setup behavior.

expectation.grounded: In Flask 2.2.0, setup-enforced application APIs on `Flask` must reject late mutations after the first request by raising `AssertionError`, including decorator-based registration paths such as `route`, `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `patch`, and `endpoint`, in addition to existing setup methods such as `add_url_rule`. On `Blueprint`, setup-oriented APIs must emit `UserWarning` once the blueprint has been registered at least once instead of silently allowing inconsistent late changes; this applies to route registration, deferred setup registration, nested blueprint registration, app-wide template registration helpers, request and teardown hooks, context processors, error handlers, and URL preprocessors/defaults. `Blueprint.before_app_first_request` must be treated as deprecated and emits `DeprecationWarning` when used, and `Blueprint.json_encoder` and `Blueprint.json_decoder` are deprecated for removal in Flask 2.3.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading, application configuration is only valid during startup, not after requests begin. Blueprint configuration is only valid before registration; if code tries to mutate a blueprint later, Flask should warn immediately that the change is too late and may not apply consistently. Blueprint-specific first-request setup should be considered deprecated and avoided.

constraints.grounded: Normal startup-time registration before the first application request and before the first blueprint registration must continue to work without new warnings or errors. Late setup must not be silently accepted: application calls must fail with `AssertionError`, while blueprint calls must emit `UserWarning`. Previously recorded blueprint setup should remain the behavior that is applied during registration rather than partially incorporating later mutations.
constraints.conceptual: Do not regress valid startup configuration flows. Only setup attempted too late in the lifecycle should be rejected or warned, and already-established application or blueprint behavior should remain stable instead of changing unpredictably.

behavior: Calling a `Flask` setup method after the application has already handled its first request now raises `AssertionError` even when debug mode is off.
Decorator-based registration helpers on `Scaffold`, including `route`, `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `patch`, and `endpoint`, now participate in the same late-setup enforcement as other setup APIs.

Calling `Blueprint` setup methods after the blueprint has been registered at least once now emits `UserWarning` instead of relying on an opt-in modification warning flag or silently accepting the change.

The blueprint warning coverage includes deferred setup registration, nested blueprint registration, URL rule registration, app-wide template filter/test/global registration, app-level request and teardown hooks, context processors, error handlers, and URL preprocessing/default handlers.
Calling `Blueprint.before_app_first_request` now emits `DeprecationWarning` in 2.2.0.
`Blueprint.json_encoder` and `Blueprint.json_decoder` are deprecated in 2.2.0 and scheduled for removal in Flask 2.3.
acceptance_criteria: When an application has already served a request and code then registers a new route or endpoint through a setup API, it should raise `AssertionError` instead of allowing the change.
When the same late application setup is attempted with `app.debug` disabled, it should still raise `AssertionError`.

When a blueprint has already been registered once and code then adds a route, hook, template registration, URL processor, or nested blueprint to it, Flask should emit `UserWarning` indicating the setup is too late to apply consistently.
When blueprint setup is completed before the blueprint is registered, it should continue to register normally without late-setup warnings.
When `Blueprint.before_app_first_request` is used, Flask should emit `DeprecationWarning`.

task_14.title: Support nested FlaskGroup CLIs
task_14.description: Flask 2.2.0 expands Flask CLI integration so a `flask.cli.FlaskGroup` can be mounted inside a larger Click command tree without losing app-factory loading, Flask CLI option and environment behavior, or access to the active application context during command execution.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that a `flask.cli.FlaskGroup` can be used as a subcommand inside a larger Click-based CLI while still loading the configured Flask application, exposing Flask and app-defined commands, and providing the expected Flask CLI runtime context.

expectation.grounded: `flask.cli.FlaskGroup` should honor its `create_app`, `load_dotenv`, and `set_debug_flag` configuration whether it is invoked directly or nested under another `click.Group`. Command lookup through `FlaskGroup` should load the application from `ScriptInfo`, continue to surface `flask.cli.NoAppException` as a CLI error when the app cannot be loaded, and, for a successfully loaded app, make the app context available so command callbacks and parameter callbacks can access `flask.current_app` without requiring `@with_appcontext`. Built-in Flask CLI options and `FLASK` environment-variable handling should remain available, including early resolution of app and env-file settings when help is shown with no explicit subcommand.
expectation.conceptual: A Flask application's CLI should behave the same whether it is the main command or a nested subcommand in a larger Click CLI: it should still find and create the app, expose the app's commands, respect normal Flask CLI environment configuration, and run nested commands with the active Flask application context available.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress existing top-level `FlaskGroup` behavior. Version option support, Flask CLI option processing, `.env` loading, `FLASK_*` environment-variable prefix handling, and debug/app configuration semantics must continue to work. If an app is already active for the same loaded application, command dispatch should not replace it with a different context; if app loading fails, command execution must not proceed as though an app were available.
constraints.conceptual: Add nesting support without changing the established behavior of the Flask CLI. Users should not need a separate standalone entry point, extra manual context setup, or different environment configuration to keep existing CLI workflows working.

behavior: A `FlaskGroup` can be registered beneath another Click group and still load the Flask app from its configured `create_app` factory instead of only working as a top-level CLI entry point.
When `FlaskGroup` resolves a command, it reports application-loading failures through the normal Flask CLI error path and does not continue command resolution against an unloaded app.

Before dispatching an app-backed command, `FlaskGroup` provides an active app context for the loaded application when one is not already active for that same app, allowing callbacks to use `flask.current_app`.

Nested `FlaskGroup` usage preserves normal Flask CLI option and environment behavior, including `.env` loading, `FLASK` auto environment-variable prefix support, and early app/env-file resolution when help is generated without a subcommand.
acceptance_criteria: Given a custom `click.Group` that includes a nested `flask.cli.FlaskGroup(create_app=...)`, when a Flask CLI command is invoked through that nested path, then the command should load the Flask application from `create_app` and run without requiring `FLASK_APP` or a separate top-level Flask entry point.
When a nested `FlaskGroup` command or its parameter callbacks access `flask.current_app`, they should observe the loaded application context during command execution.
When a `FlaskGroup` is invoked with no subcommand and help output is produced, application commands should still be discoverable when app selection comes from Flask CLI environment configuration.

When the configured Flask application cannot be loaded for a `FlaskGroup`, the CLI should fail through normal Flask CLI error reporting and should not execute the requested command against a missing app.

task_16.title: Support explicit dotenv files in the Flask CLI
task_16.description: Flask 2.2.0 adds an explicit CLI option for loading a user-selected dotenv file during startup. This lets applications receive configuration from a chosen env file in addition to the default dotenv sources, with the file loaded early enough to affect application selection and startup behavior. Invalid env-file usage is surfaced as CLI parameter validation rather than being ignored.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the `flask` CLI allows users to provide an explicit environment file to load at startup, so applications can be configured from a chosen dotenv file in addition to the default dotenv loading behavior.

expectation.grounded: The `flask` CLI should accept `-e` and `--env-file` on `FlaskGroup` and load environment variables from the provided file through `python-dotenv` before later CLI option handling and app loading. This explicit env file should be additive with the normal `.env` and `.flaskenv` loading behavior rather than replacing it. If explicit env-file loading is requested when `python-dotenv` is unavailable, the CLI should fail with `click.BadParameter` instead of continuing silently.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to launch Flask commands with a specific dotenv file and have those values available immediately during startup. The explicitly selected file should complement the usual dotenv sources, and unsupported usage should be rejected as an invalid CLI parameter.

constraints.grounded: The `--env-file` value should resolve to an existing file and should be processed early enough to influence app resolution and startup configuration. Adding this option must not regress existing `flask` CLI behaviors for application selection or debug-related startup behavior, and an explicitly supplied env file should not be suppressed by the automatic dotenv skip setting that only controls default file discovery.
constraints.conceptual: The new CLI capability should be additive and non-breaking: existing startup flows must keep working, while explicit env-file loading is validated and applied predictably before the app begins loading.

behavior: The `flask` CLI accepts a new `-e` or `--env-file` option for specifying a dotenv file to load.
When an env file is provided, its variables are loaded before subsequent app and startup option processing so they can affect application startup.
The explicit env file is loaded in addition to the standard `.env` and `.flaskenv` behavior rather than replacing those sources.
An explicitly requested env file is still honored even when automatic dotenv discovery is otherwise skipped.
If `python-dotenv` is not installed and explicit env-file loading is requested, the CLI raises a parameter validation error.
If the supplied env-file path is not an existing file, the CLI rejects the option as invalid input.
acceptance_criteria: When a user runs a Flask CLI command with `--env-file` pointing to a valid dotenv file, the command should load that file's environment variables before the application is resolved and started.
When `.env` or `.flaskenv` are also present, providing `--env-file` should add the specified file as another configuration source instead of disabling the default dotenv behavior.
When automatic dotenv loading is disabled but a user explicitly provides `--env-file`, the specified file should still be loaded.
When `--env-file` is used without `python-dotenv` being installed, the CLI should fail with a parameter error rather than ignoring the request.
When `--env-file` points to a path that does not exist or is not a file, the CLI should reject the command before application startup.

task_17.title: Provide app context automatically for Flask CLI callbacks
task_17.description: Flask CLI now activates the application context earlier for commands registered on app.cli or blueprint.cli, so argument and option callbacks, subcommands, and command bodies can use application-scoped state without requiring explicit @with_appcontext decoration.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that custom Flask CLI commands have an active application context for the full command lifecycle, including parameter callback evaluation, so application-scoped objects can be used without extra context decorators.

expectation.grounded: Commands registered through app.cli or blueprint.cli must have the loaded Flask application's context active before Click parameter callbacks and command callbacks run. Accessing current_app from those callbacks should succeed without adding @with_appcontext, and current_app should correspond to the app loaded for that CLI invocation. The with_appcontext decorator must remain usable for callbacks that still need to ensure an application context explicitly.
expectation.conceptual: Invoking a Flask CLI command should make application-scoped state available consistently from argument parsing through command execution. Users should no longer need extra decorator boilerplate just to access app configuration, database-backed helpers, or other app-bound objects inside CLI callbacks.

constraints.grounded: Do not require @with_appcontext on commands or parameter callbacks registered on app.cli or blueprint.cli solely to access application context. Preserve compatibility for existing explicit with_appcontext usage, and do not switch to a different app instance between callback parsing and command execution during the same invocation. Application-loading failures should still surface as command load errors rather than being hidden by the new context behavior.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should remove unnecessary context setup for supported Flask CLI commands without breaking existing commands that already opt into explicit app-context handling. It should keep command execution tied to the same application instance and should not mask failures to load the application.

behavior: A Flask application context is established before Click evaluates argument or option callbacks for commands loaded from app.cli or blueprint.cli.
Parameter callbacks for those commands can access current_app and other application-context-bound resources without failing due to missing application context.
Command callbacks and subcommands execute under the same loaded Flask application that was made active during command resolution.
with_appcontext remains supported, but when an application context is already active it should reuse that context instead of requiring a second explicit context setup.
acceptance_criteria: When a custom command is registered on app.cli or blueprint.cli and one of its Click argument or option callbacks accesses current_app, invoking the command should complete without requiring @with_appcontext on that callback.
When a custom Flask CLI command accesses application-scoped state in its command body, it should observe the same loaded application that was active during parameter parsing.
When a supported CLI subcommand is invoked, it should have application context available during its execution without additional decoration.
When an existing callback is still wrapped with with_appcontext, it should continue to run successfully whether or not the command already entered an application context.

task_18.title: Adopt timezone-aware session expiration timestamps
task_18.description: The session expiration API now produces timezone-aware UTC datetimes for permanent sessions instead of naive UTC datetimes. This aligns expiration handling with modern datetime expectations while preserving the same lifetime-based expiration moment and the existing no-expiration behavior for non-permanent sessions.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that permanent session expiration values are exposed as timezone-aware UTC datetimes instead of naive UTC datetimes, while preserving the same expiration timing semantics and continuing to report no expiration for non-permanent sessions.

expectation.grounded: In Flask 2.2.0, `SessionInterface.get_expiration_time(app, session)` should return a UTC-aware `datetime` when `session.permanent` is true, computed from the current UTC time plus `app.permanent_session_lifetime`. When `session.permanent` is false, it should still return `None`. Any application or extension code that reads, compares, serializes, or propagates this API's return value should treat it as an aware UTC timestamp.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading, permanent-session expiration timestamps should carry explicit UTC timezone information rather than being timezone-naive. The expiration deadline itself should remain the same logical UTC-based moment, and sessions without permanence should continue to have no expiration timestamp.

constraints.grounded: Do not change which sessions receive an expiration value: only permanent sessions should produce one, and non-permanent sessions must continue to yield `None`. Preserve calculation from the configured permanent lifetime and keep the expiration reference in UTC rather than introducing a different timezone or shifting the effective expiration instant.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should change timezone metadata, not the intended lifespan of a permanent session. Existing session expiration behavior should remain stable except that the exposed timestamp is now explicitly UTC-aware.

behavior: Calling `SessionInterface.get_expiration_time` for a permanent session returns a timezone-aware UTC `datetime`.
The expiration timestamp is still derived from the current UTC time plus the configured permanent session lifetime.
Calling `SessionInterface.get_expiration_time` for a non-permanent session continues to return `None`.
Application and extension code that consumes session expiration values must handle aware UTC datetimes instead of naive datetimes.
acceptance_criteria: When a permanent session's expiration time is requested, it should expose a `datetime` with UTC timezone information representing the current UTC time plus the configured permanent lifetime.
When a non-permanent session's expiration time is requested, it should report no expiration timestamp.

When expiration metadata is consumed by application code, custom session backends, or cookie-setting flows, it should represent the same expiration instant as before the upgrade while retaining explicit UTC timezone awareness.

task_15.title: Expose explicit Flask CLI app, debug, and env-file options
task_15.description: The Flask CLI now supports selecting the application with `--app`, controlling debug mode with `--debug` or `--no-debug`, and loading variables from an explicit env file before application discovery. This makes CLI startup less dependent on pre-exported environment variables and improves how help and missing-app guidance reflect the configured app source.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the `flask` CLI lets users choose the application and debug mode directly from command-line options, and optionally load environment variables from a specific env file early enough for app discovery, help output, and command execution, without requiring environment-variable-only setup.

expectation.grounded: The `flask` command should accept `-A`/`--app` for selecting the Flask application or factory to load, accept `--debug` and `--no-debug` for explicit debug control, and accept `-e`/`--env-file` for loading environment variables before app resolution. `--app` should support the documented import target forms for Flask app loading, while missing-app guidance should point users to `--app`, `FLASK_APP`, or fallback discovery from `wsgi.py` or `app.py`. If an explicit env file is requested and `python-dotenv` is unavailable, the CLI should raise a parameter error instead of silently ignoring the option.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to run Flask CLI commands by naming the app and debug mode directly on the command line, and they should be able to point the CLI at a specific env file when startup configuration lives outside the default environment. The CLI should resolve that configuration early enough that command help, app loading, and error reporting all reflect the chosen app and debug settings.

constraints.grounded: Omitting `--app` and `--debug` must not break existing environment-based behavior: `FLASK_APP`, `FLASK_DEBUG`, automatic `.env` and `.flaskenv` loading, and default discovery from `wsgi.py` or `app.py` should still be honored. Explicit `--debug` or `--no-debug` should only override debug behavior when the option is actually provided, not when the option remains at its default value. `--env-file` should require an existing file and should load it even when automatic dotenv loading is otherwise skipped.
constraints.conceptual: The new CLI flags should extend startup configuration without removing the old ways of configuring Flask. Explicit command-line choices should take precedence when provided, but the CLI should continue to behave like earlier versions when users rely on environment variables or default app discovery.

behavior: The `flask` CLI accepts `-A` and `--app` so the application or factory can be selected directly from the command line instead of requiring `FLASK_APP` to be set in advance.
The `flask` CLI accepts `--debug` and `--no-debug` to explicitly enable or disable debug mode from the command line.
When debug is explicitly set through the CLI, that state is available early enough for factory-based app loading and other startup logic that reads `FLASK_DEBUG`.
The `-e` and `--env-file` option loads environment variables from a specific file before the app is resolved, so values from that file can affect application selection and debug mode.
If `python-dotenv` is not installed, using `--env-file` produces a CLI parameter error instead of falling back silently.

Help and missing-app behavior reflect the new CLI configuration path: application-defined commands can be discovered from early app/env resolution, and missing-app guidance points users to `--app`, `FLASK_APP`, or default file discovery.
acceptance_criteria: When a user runs a Flask CLI command with `--app` or `-A`, the command should load the targeted application or factory without requiring `FLASK_APP` to be exported first.
When a user runs a Flask CLI command with `--debug`, it should execute with debug mode explicitly enabled; when run with `--no-debug`, it should execute with debug mode explicitly disabled.
When the user does not provide a debug flag, the CLI should continue to rely on existing environment-based debug configuration rather than forcing a new default.

When a user provides `--env-file` with a valid file, variables from that file should be loaded before application discovery so settings such as app selection and debug mode can influence command execution and help output.
When `--env-file` is used without `python-dotenv` being available, the CLI should fail with an option-level error that indicates the dependency is required.
When no application can be resolved, the CLI should report that the user can supply `--app`, use `FLASK_APP`, or rely on `wsgi.py` or `app.py` in the current directory.

task_19.title: Support direct streaming returns from view functions
task_19.description: The 2.2.0 upgrade improves streaming response ergonomics. Applications can return iterators or generators directly from Flask view functions and have them converted through the normal response pipeline, and the release also introduces helper APIs for streaming template output progressively.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Flask 2.2.0 enables first-class streaming responses by allowing view functions to return iterators or generators directly, while also exposing helper APIs for progressively rendering templates without requiring manual response wrapping.

expectation.grounded: Flask should treat direct view return values that are iterators, including Iterator[str] and Iterator[bytes], as valid response bodies and convert them with the app's response class so normal status and header handling still applies. The upgrade also includes public streaming helpers `stream_template` and `stream_template_string` for incremental template rendering with the appropriate Flask context.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to stream response content by returning a generator or iterator from a view, without having to manually construct a Response first. Template output should also be streamable through dedicated helper functions that preserve normal Flask rendering context.

constraints.grounded: Existing response handling for Response objects, plain text or bytes bodies, and JSON-style mapping or list return values should remain compatible. Direct iterator returns should go through the same response-class conversion path used for other simple body values, preserving standard defaults instead of introducing a separate calling convention.
constraints.conceptual: The new streaming capability should extend existing response behavior rather than replace it. Non-streaming return types must keep working as before, and streamed responses should follow the same default HTTP behavior users already expect from Flask.

behavior: A Flask view may return an iterator or generator directly instead of wrapping it in a Response object.
Iterators yielding text chunks are accepted as response bodies and converted through the app's standard response class.
