Iterators yielding byte chunks are accepted as response bodies and converted through the app's standard response class.
Direct iterator returns continue to receive normal response defaults such as the usual status code and header processing supplied by the configured response class.
The public response-value typing for view returns recognizes iterators alongside existing mapping and list style return values.
Template streaming is available through `stream_template` and `stream_template_string`, which are intended for progressive rendering under the correct Flask context.
acceptance_criteria: When a view returns a generator or iterator of strings, Flask should serve it as a valid HTTP response without requiring the view to manually create a Response object.
When a view returns a generator or iterator of bytes, Flask should serve it as a valid HTTP response without requiring manual response wrapping.
When a direct iterator return is used, the response should still use the application's normal response defaults for status and headers unless the view explicitly overrides them.
When an application uses `stream_template` or `stream_template_string`, template output should be produced incrementally while preserving normal Flask rendering context.

task_20.title: Add streaming template rendering helpers
task_20.description: Flask 2.2.0 adds first-class helpers for streaming Jinja template output so applications can return template content incrementally instead of rendering the entire response up front. The new APIs preserve normal template context behavior and render lifecycle signaling while making streamed responses easier to build.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications can render Jinja templates incrementally for streaming HTTP responses through supported Flask helper APIs, while preserving the same template context behavior developers expect from normal template rendering.

expectation.grounded: Expose `stream_template` and `stream_template_string` as public Flask APIs alongside `render_template` and `render_template_string`. Each streaming API should resolve the target template or template source through the current application, apply template context updates before rendering begins, and return an iterator of string chunks rather than a fully rendered string. When used during an active request, the streamed iterator should retain request context for the duration of generation. Template render lifecycle signals should remain observable, with the pre-render signal occurring before streaming starts and the completion signal occurring only after the stream has been fully consumed.
expectation.conceptual: Developers should be able to choose between full template rendering and streaming template rendering using official Flask helpers. Streaming should emit the response piece by piece, preserve normal template context behavior, and keep request-bound data available until the streamed output finishes.

constraints.grounded: `render_template` and `render_template_string` must continue to return complete rendered strings. The new streaming helpers must work for both named templates and inline template source, depend on the active application context, and preserve request-aware behavior while the iterator is being consumed. Stream completion must not be reported before generation actually finishes.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must add incremental template rendering without regressing existing non-streaming rendering behavior. Streamed templates should behave like normal templating from the caller's perspective, except that output is produced lazily and remains safe to use in request-driven responses.

behavior: `stream_template` renders a named template, or the first available template from a provided list, as an iterator of string fragments.
`stream_template_string` renders an inline template source as an iterator of string fragments.
Both streaming helpers apply the application's template context updates before any output is generated.
When a request is active, consuming the streamed iterator preserves request context for the full duration of generation.
The template pre-render signal is emitted before streaming starts, and the template-rendered signal is emitted only after the iterator finishes producing output.
acceptance_criteria: When an application calls `stream_template` for a valid template and returns it from a view, the client should receive the rendered template content as a streamed response instead of requiring the entire template to be built first.
When an application calls `stream_template_string`, the rendered output should be produced incrementally and match the same template data that full rendering would expose.
When template context processors or application-provided context are involved, streamed templates should receive that context the same way non-streamed templates do.
When streamed template generation depends on request-bound objects, those objects should remain accessible until the stream has been fully consumed.
When observers rely on template render lifecycle signals, they should receive the start-of-render signal before output begins and the completion signal only after streaming completes.

task_21.title: Adopt Flask 2.2 context preservation semantics
task_21.description: Flask 2.2 replaces its preserved request-context behavior for the debugger and test client so that request and application context locals are restored with the correct data after the request ends, while teardown now always runs at request completion. This also separates streamed response context cleanup from test-client block cleanup and deprecates the `Flask.propagate_exceptions` property accessor.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Flask 2.2 preserves `request`, `g`, and related context-local objects with the correct request-specific data in the interactive debugger and test client, while still running request teardown at the end of every request and cleaning up streamed contexts only when the streamed response is consumed or closed. Ensure that code relying on `Flask.propagate_exceptions` accounts for its deprecation.

expectation.grounded: When Flask preserves context for the interactive debugger or `FlaskClient`, `request`, `g`, and other context-local proxies should resolve against the correct preserved request after the request has already been popped. `teardown_request` handlers must run when the request ends even if the context is preserved, and must run again when a preserved context is later popped. A context created by `stream_with_context` must be preserved independently from a `with client` block and cleaned up when the response body is consumed with `response.get_data()` / `response.data` or when `response.close()` is called. Accessing `Flask.propagate_exceptions` should emit a `DeprecationWarning` in 2.2.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, preserved request state should still be available in debugging and client-inspection flows, but request teardown should no longer be delayed just because that state remains inspectable. Streamed responses should keep their own context alive only until the stream is consumed or explicitly closed. Any use of the exception-propagation convenience accessor should be treated as deprecated.

constraints.grounded: Do not rely on preserved request contexts remaining active on the live context stack after request dispatch completes. Do not assume teardown is deferred until the next request. Do not let a `with client` block pop unrelated preserved contexts such as a `stream_with_context` response. Preserve existing `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` config behavior, while treating the `Flask.propagate_exceptions` property as deprecated rather than changing the runtime exception-propagation outcome.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must avoid leaking request context or cleanup work across requests, must keep independently preserved contexts isolated from one another, and must not change exception propagation behavior except for surfacing deprecation on the legacy accessor.

behavior: Flask now pops the request context at the end of request handling even when context preservation is active for debugging or the test client.

If debugging context preservation is enabled, the preserved application and request contexts are recorded and later re-entered so that `request`, `g`, and other context-local proxies point to the correct request-specific data.
`teardown_request` execution is tied to request-context popping, so teardown runs at request end even for preserved contexts, and runs again when a preserved context is later exited.
`FlaskClient` preserves contexts by re-entering recorded context managers after the response is created, instead of leaving the original request context on the stack until a later request.
Before each client request, previously preserved client contexts are closed so they do not leak across redirects or multiple requests in the same client block.
`stream_with_context` cleanup is independent from `with client`; its preserved context remains until the response body is read or the response is explicitly closed.
Accessing the `Flask.propagate_exceptions` property now emits a `DeprecationWarning`; the `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` configuration value still determines behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When a request is inspected in Flask's interactive debugger after request handling has finished, `request` and other context-local proxies should reflect the request that triggered the debugger, including in threaded execution.

When a request handled through `FlaskClient` completes inside a `with client` block, request teardown should already have run for that request even though the preserved context remains available for inspection.
When a preserved client context is later exited, teardown associated with popping that preserved context should run again without requiring a subsequent request to trigger cleanup.

When a streamed response uses `stream_with_context` inside a `with client` block, leaving the client block should not consume or close the streamed context; that cleanup should happen only after reading the response body or explicitly closing the response.
When multiple requests or redirects occur through the same `FlaskClient`, preserved contexts from earlier requests should not remain active and should not affect later requests.
When application code accesses `Flask.propagate_exceptions`, it should receive the current propagation setting while also observing that the accessor is deprecated.

task_22.title: Support direct JSON array responses from Flask view functions
task_22.description: Flask 2.2.0 expands automatic response conversion so a view can return a Python list and have it serialized as a JSON response, aligning array payloads with the existing dict-to-JSON behavior. The upgrade also clarifies the accepted response-type contract around list values and tuple shortcuts.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to Flask 2.2.0 can return JSON array payloads directly from view functions, with the same automatic JSON response handling previously available for dictionary return values, while preserving the existing tuple-based status and header shortcuts.

expectation.grounded: Flask view functions should accept `list` return values as valid `ResponseValue` outputs and convert them into JSON responses through the same response-coercion path used for `dict` values. If a view returns a tuple whose primary value is a `list`, Flask should still apply tuple-based status or header handling after coercing the list body into a response. Response-type validation should treat `list` as a supported return type, and invalid-return errors should describe tuples specifically as shortcuts for status and/or headers rather than as arbitrary response bodies.
expectation.conceptual: A Flask endpoint may return a plain Python list to produce a JSON array response, and this should behave consistently with the framework's existing automatic JSON handling for object-like payloads. Returning a list should no longer be treated as an invalid response, and combining that payload with normal status or header shortcuts should continue to work.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress existing response coercion for strings, bytes, dictionaries, `Response` objects, or WSGI callables. Only list values are newly accepted for automatic JSON conversion; tuple handling must remain limited to status/header response shortcuts, and broader mapping or iterator typing support must not be interpreted as changing the runtime rule that JSON auto-conversion is keyed to concrete dict and list return bodies.
constraints.conceptual: Existing valid response forms must keep their current behavior. The new support should add JSON array returns without changing the meaning of tuple response shortcuts or widening runtime acceptance beyond the response shapes the framework already documents.

behavior: Returning a plain Python list from a Flask view produces a JSON response instead of a response-type error.
List return values are serialized through the framework's automatic JSON response machinery in the same way dictionary return values are.
A tuple response that uses a list as its body still supports the normal status-code or header shortcut semantics.

When Flask rejects an unsupported view return value, the reported set of valid response categories now includes list values and clarifies that tuples are only valid when used for status and/or headers.
The public response typing contract is broadened to reflect list-based response bodies alongside the existing supported response shapes.
acceptance_criteria: When a view function returns a Python list, the request should complete with a JSON array response rather than raising an invalid response type error.
When a view function returns a tuple containing a Python list and an HTTP status, the response should preserve the requested status and serialize the list as JSON.
When a view function returns a tuple containing a Python list and response headers, the response should include those headers and serialize the list as JSON.
When a view function returns a dictionary, it should continue to produce a JSON response exactly as before.
When a view function returns an unsupported type, the resulting error should identify list returns as valid and describe tuple returns as valid only for status and header shortcuts.

task_23.title: Broaden Flask view return type annotations
task_23.description: Flask 2.2.0 expands the public response return typing contract so route and view functions can be annotated with additional runtime-supported response shapes, especially TypedDict-backed JSON payloads, without static type checker rejection.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask view functions can declare runtime-supported response return types, including TypedDict-based JSON objects, without being rejected by the framework's public typing contract after upgrading from 2.1.3.

expectation.grounded: The public `ResponseValue` type used by Flask route decorators and view callables should accept mapping-shaped return annotations so `TypedDict` return types are valid, and it should also cover list and string-or-bytes iterator return annotations that Flask already supports as responses. Annotating a route or view to return these types should no longer produce type incompatibility errors solely because of Flask's type definitions.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to use precise type annotations for valid Flask responses, including structured JSON objects and streamed content, without having to widen those annotations just to satisfy static type checking.

constraints.grounded: Existing valid return annotations such as `Response`, `str`, and `bytes` must remain accepted. The change must be limited to Flask's exposed typing contract and must not imply new runtime response-conversion behavior beyond values Flask already handles.
constraints.conceptual: Keep current response behavior intact while making the declared type surface accurately reflect supported response forms. Previously valid annotations must continue to work.

behavior: Flask's response return typing accepts mapping-style annotations, allowing `TypedDict` return types to be used for route and view functions without static type checker rejection.
Flask's response return typing accepts list return annotations for response values that are already supported at runtime.
Flask's response return typing accepts `Iterator[str]` and `Iterator[bytes]` return annotations for streamed response values.
Previously accepted response annotations such as `Response`, `str`, and `bytes` remain part of the supported return type contract.
acceptance_criteria: When a route or view function is annotated to return a `TypedDict`-compatible JSON object, Flask's public typing should treat that callable as a valid response producer.

When a route or view function is annotated to return a list response value that Flask already converts successfully at runtime, the annotation should be accepted by the framework's typing definitions.
When a route or view function is annotated to return `Iterator[str]` or `Iterator[bytes]` for streaming output, the annotation should be accepted as a valid response type.
When existing routes are annotated to return `Response`, `str`, or `bytes`, their typing compatibility should remain unchanged after the upgrade.

task_24.title: Remove flask run eager/lazy loading toggle and standardize app loading
task_24.description: Flask 2.2.0 removes the `--eager-loading/--lazy-loading` switch from `flask run` and makes application loading consistent: the app is loaded immediately on the initial command invocation so startup errors surface right away, while reload cycles still tolerate load failures and keep the reloader active.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `flask run` no longer exposes a lazy-versus-eager loading toggle. Ensure that the first application load happens immediately when the command starts so startup failures are reported at launch time. Ensure that reloads still recover from application import or factory errors without terminating the reloader. Ensure that invoking `app.run()` from code while the app is already being run through the Flask CLI does not start a second blocking server.

expectation.grounded: The `flask run` command must stop accepting the `--eager-loading/--lazy-loading` option pair. `flask run` must call the application loader before starting the server. If `info.load_app()` fails during the initial non-reloader invocation, the command should raise that exception immediately and fail startup. If `info.load_app()` fails while running from the reloader, the traceback should be printed immediately and the serving process should remain available so the stored exception is raised later by the request-handling app callable. When `Flask.run()` is reached while `FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI` indicates the app is being launched by the Flask CLI, it should be ignored instead of starting another server, and an interactive terminal notice should be shown on the initial process.
expectation.conceptual: Users should no longer choose between eager and lazy loading for `flask run`; the command should behave consistently by loading the app up front on startup. Startup errors should appear as soon as the command is run. During automatic reloads, load errors should still be surfaced immediately without killing the reloader, so fixing the code and saving should allow the app to recover. If application code calls `app.run()` while the Flask CLI is already managing the server, Flask should ignore that nested server start rather than blocking or creating duplicate servers.

constraints.grounded: Do not preserve any public CLI path that allows toggling load mode for `flask run`. Preserve the distinction between first startup and reload-time behavior: initial startup failures abort the command, whereas reloader failures are surfaced immediately but do not disable the reload loop. `Flask.run()` must remain callable outside the Flask CLI, and only be ignored when the CLI-run environment marker is present.
constraints.conceptual: Do not leave multiple supported startup modes for the development server. Keep immediate failure reporting for normal startup, but keep reload resilience for edit-and-refresh workflows. Avoid breaking direct programmatic server startup outside the CLI-managed case.

behavior: `flask run` no longer provides `--eager-loading` or `--lazy-loading` as user-selectable options.
The application is loaded before the development server starts on the initial command execution.
An application load failure on initial startup causes `flask run` to fail immediately instead of waiting until the first request.
An application load failure during a reload prints the error immediately and keeps the reloader active so the server can recover after code changes.
If `app.run()` is invoked while the app is already being started through the Flask CLI, Flask ignores that call instead of starting an additional blocking server process.
acceptance_criteria: When a user upgrades to 2.2.0 and invokes `flask run`, the command should not accept `--eager-loading` or `--lazy-loading`.
When the application cannot be imported or created on the first `flask run` startup, the command should surface the failure immediately and exit without waiting for a request.
When the application fails to load during a reload cycle, the error should be shown immediately and the reload process should continue running so a later code fix can restore the app.
When application code contains `app.run()` and the server is launched with `flask run`, Flask should ignore that nested call rather than starting a second server.
When `app.run()` is used directly outside the Flask CLI workflow, it should continue to start the development server normally.
